reasons: The tests are clear, but they use a fake model, so they do not show real model output is safe.

terms.meaning: A small piece of code that runs the app with set inputs and checks the result is what is expected.
A reusable setup helper that tests can ask for, such as the sample future state.
A fake stand-in for the real model connection that returns chosen replies.
Running one test several times, once for each example in a list.
An error raised when the agent says something it is not allowed to say.
Code that can wait for slow work, such as a model call, without freezing the program.
A label pointing to a source record that backs up a claim.

used_by: pytest (runs the test file directly; no other callers visible)

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and test setup
sections.what: Loads the agent, the schema types, the fake client helpers, and marks every test to run asynchronously.
sections.why: Shared setup needed by all the tests below.
sections.watch_out: The tests depend on exact names from the schema package, so renaming one breaks the whole file.

sections.name: anyio_backend
sections.title: Async engine choice
sections.what: Tells the test runner to run these async tests on the asyncio engine.
sections.why: Likely reason: asyncio is the async engine the project uses.

sections.name: future_state
sections.title: Sample future-state input
sections.what: Builds one realistic future-state description with one step, one agent, a moderate posture, and an exception plan, which each test feeds to the agent.
sections.why: Gives every test the same realistic input so only the tested detail changes.
sections.watch_out: Changing any field here changes the input for every test in the file.

sections.name: output
sections.title: Sample model reply
sections.what: Builds a fake model reply with one operating-model line and one workforce line that has a role, a headcount direction, skill changes, and citations.
sections.why: Lets each test change just the role or skill text it cares about.
sections.watch_out: The default skill text is used by many tests, so altering it changes what they check.

sections.name: TestHappyPath
sections.title: Normal-case tests
sections.what: Checks that a normal reply comes back as implications, that the direction survives, that the request goes to the standard model tier, and that every allowed direction word is listed in the task text sent to the model.
sections.watch_out: The model tier check depends on the routing table, so changing routing changes this test.

sections.name: TestNoQuantification (part 1)
sections.title: Schema and quantity-rejection tests
sections.what: Checks that the workforce schema has no field for headcount or effort totals, and that quantified text in descriptions or skill changes is rejected as a boundary violation.
sections.why: The docstring says totals belong elsewhere, so a number here would be a second, competing total.
sections.watch_out: The rejection only catches the wordings listed in the tests, so new phrasings can get through.

sections.name: TestNoQuantification: test_unquantified_prose_passes
sections.title: Plain-wording pass tests and task-text rule
sections.what: Checks that plain statements about ownership or roles come back unchanged, and that the task text contains the explicit instructions to avoid stating savings and to give directions only.
sections.why: Stops the number check from being so strict that it rejects normal wording. The task-text check guards the instructions given to the model.
sections.watch_out: If the number check is tightened, these examples are what catch false rejections.

sections.name: TestFailurePaths
sections.title: Failure-path tests
sections.what: Checks that an invented evidence id is rejected with a validation error naming that id, and that a reply with no evidence still produces implications.
sections.why: Evidence ids must point to real records. The reason the empty-evidence case should still pass is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The rejection test sends the bad reply twice. The reason for the second copy is not stated in the code.

summary: Checks that the workforce modeller agent describes direction of change only, never a number of people or effort, and that it rejects citations to evidence that does not exist.
purpose: Tests the `WorkforceModeller` agent using a fake model client, so no real model is called.
why: Effort and headcount totals are computed in another package. If this agent stated a number, the app would show two conflicting totals, so the rule is enforced by tests.
how: Each test builds a sample future-state description and a fake model reply, runs the agent, and checks the result. Replies containing quantities should raise a boundary error. Replies citing unknown evidence ids should raise a validation error. Plain wording should pass unchanged.
inputs: A sample future-state description, fake model replies built in this file, and a sample run context.
outputs: Pass or fail results from pytest. The file writes no files.
risks: The fake client skips the real model, so these tests show the checks work but not how the model behaves. The number check only catches the wordings listed in the tests.
debug: If a quantity test stops failing, look at the boundary check in the workforce modeller module and the list of quantity patterns it uses. If the task-text test fails, check the wording in `TASK_TEMPLATE`.
